intro: Spam complaint rate is the share of delivered emails a recipient reported as spam instead of simply ignoring or unsubscribing. Enter complaints and delivered emails to get the rate.

sections.heading: How Complaint Rate is calculated
sections.body: Complaint Rate = Complaints ÷ Delivered Emails. Delivered, not sent, is the denominator — a bounced message was never in a position to be reported as spam, so it shouldn't count toward the total this rate is measured against.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: 5 ÷ 10,000 = 0.05%. A tiny-looking percentage, but complaint rate is one of the few email metrics where mailbox providers themselves publish specific thresholds — the scale here matters more than it does for most other rates.

sections.heading: Why complaint rate gets more scrutiny than other list metrics
sections.body: [Google's own Gmail bulk sender guidelines set explicit thresholds on this kind of rate: senders are told to keep it below 0.1%, and rates of 0.3% or higher make a bulk sender ineligible for delivery mitigation](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/14229414?hl=en). That's a real, sourced threshold from a mailbox provider, not a marketing benchmark — it applies specifically to bulk senders under Gmail's own guidelines and its own measurement methodology, which isn't guaranteed to use the identical delivered-based formula this calculator does. A high complaint rate affects whether a mailbox provider trusts a sender at all, which is a different and more consequential kind of signal than most engagement metrics carry.

sections.heading: Complaint Rate vs. Unsubscribe Rate
sections.body: Both mean a recipient didn't want the email, but they carry very different weight. [Unsubscribe Rate](/calculators/unsubscribe-rate) reflects the intended, expected opt-out path — a normal outcome at some baseline rate. Complaint Rate reflects a recipient reaching for "Report spam" instead of the unsubscribe link, which mailbox providers treat as a much stronger signal against the sender's reputation. A rising complaint rate alongside a flat unsubscribe rate can mean the unsubscribe process itself is hard to find, pushing recipients toward the spam button as the easier option.

faq.a: Spam complaint rate is the percentage of delivered emails that a recipient reported as spam rather than ignoring or unsubscribing, calculated as complaints divided by delivered emails. It's tracked separately from unsubscribe rate because mailbox providers treat a spam report as a much stronger negative signal about a sender's trustworthiness. Complaint rate is one of the few email metrics with an explicit, mailbox-provider-published threshold: Google's own Gmail bulk sender guidelines call for keeping this kind of rate below 0.1%, with 0.3% or higher triggering real delivery consequences. A single spam complaint carries far more weight against sender reputation than a single unsubscribe, which is why even a small increase in this rate is worth investigating quickly.

faq.q: How do you calculate Complaint Rate?
faq.a: Divide complaints by delivered emails: Complaint Rate = Complaints ÷ Delivered. A campaign delivered to 10,000 recipients with 5 spam complaints has a complaint rate of 5 ÷ 10,000 = 0.05%. Delivered, not sent, is the correct denominator, since a bounced email was never received and couldn't have been reported. Both figures need to come from the same send and reporting window, and complaints should never exceed delivered emails, since every complaint implies the message actually reached the recipient first. Most email service providers report this figure automatically through feedback loops with major mailbox providers, so it rarely needs manual tracking.

faq.q: Is there an official complaint rate threshold to worry about?
faq.a: Yes, from mailbox providers themselves rather than a marketing rule of thumb. Google's Gmail bulk sender guidelines state that senders should keep their spam-report rate below 0.1%, and that rates reaching 0.3% or higher make a bulk sender ineligible for Gmail's delivery mitigation support. That's a real, published threshold specific to Gmail's own bulk-sender enforcement, measured through Gmail's own methodology — it's a useful reference point for how seriously mailbox providers take this metric, but it isn't a universal benchmark every complaint rate figure should be judged against regardless of context or measurement method. Other major mailbox providers run their own complaint feedback-loop and reputation programs with their own policies, which aren't guaranteed to mirror Gmail's specific numbers.
